content: 1. In settings with a high prevalence of tuberculosis (TB), children and adolescents who visit healthcare facilities are at risk of acquiring TB, and adolescents themselves may pose a risk of transmitting the disease. Infants, young children, and children or adolescents living with HIV are particularly vulnerable to developing TB after exposure. 2. Individuals with suspected or confirmed TB should not share waiting areas with infants attending immunization or well-baby checkups, nor with children and adolescents at HIV clinics. Children and adolescents with cavitary or sputum smear-positive TB should be isolated to prevent transmission. 3. The risk of TB exposure is especially high in facilities that care for adults with TB and/or HIV, as TB is the most common opportunistic infection in adults living with HIV, particularly those of childbearing or parenting age. 4. While children with TB are often considered non-infectious, adolescents and, in some cases, younger children can transmit TB. Infection control measures are therefore critical in healthcare settings, especially in areas dedicated to managing children. 5. The highest risk of TB transmission occurs in areas where young, vulnerable children mix with untreated adults and adolescents with presumptive TB. Additionally, there is a significant risk of undiagnosed and untreated TB among adults accompanying or visiting these children. 6. The clinical presentation of TB in children is variable and often overlaps with conditions such as pneumonia, HIV, and malnutrition. As a result, infection control measures are relevant in all outpatient and inpatient areas where children receive care. 7. Specific high-risk areas include neonatal care settings (where neonates are highly vulnerable to severe TB disease), healthcare facilities for adults and adolescents with presumptive TB, antenatal care settings, HIV clinics, facilities for children with severe malnutrition, and other congregate settings such as childcare facilities, orphanages, prisons, and schools. 8. School-aged children with bacteriologically confirmed TB should not attend school until they are no longer infectious, typically two weeks after starting effective treatment for drug-susceptible TB. However, it is important for children and adolescents with TB to return to school as soon as they are well enough, to minimize disruption to their education. School management should be informed, and mask-wearing is not required for non-infectious children. 9. Children in displaced and mobile populations, such as those in migrant labor camps, crowded refugee camps, and temporary shelters, are at heightened risk of TB exposure and infection. 10. The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine is recommended for neonates in high-incidence settings and high-risk neonates in low-incidence settings. Timing of BCG administration is particularly important for infants exposed to HIV or born to mothers with infectious TB. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends TB preventive treatment (TPT) to reduce the risk of progression from TB infection to active TB disease. Target groups for TPT include individuals at increased risk of progression to TB disease and those with a higher likelihood of TB exposure or infection. 12. Shorter, child-friendly TPT regimens are recommended for children, and the choice of regimen depends on factors such as age, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, and the availability of suitable formulations. 13. TB infection prevention and control in healthcare facilities is crucial and involves administrative and environmental controls as well as respiratory protection. 14. Diagnosing TB in children and adolescents requires careful clinical assessment supported by relevant tests and investigations. Young children often have paucibacillary disease, making bacteriological tests less sensitive in this age group compared to older adolescents and adults. 15. Alternative sample types that can be collected less invasively are important for obtaining bacteriological confirmation in young children, who may not be able to produce sputum samples easily. 16. Pulmonary TB (PTB) refers to any bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB involving the lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree. Miliary TB is classified as PTB due to lung involvement, while tuberculous pleural effusion without lung abnormalities is classified as extrapulmonary TB (EPTB). 17. The most common clinical presentation of PTB in children includes persistent cough and poor weight gain. In high-risk groups, such as children living with HIV and infants, PTB may present as acute pneumonia. 18. A history of close contact with a person with TB, particularly bacteriologically confirmed TB, is a significant risk factor for TB in children and adolescents. Contact investigations should identify the source case, assess their drug resistance pattern, and evaluate any household members with chronic cough for possible TB. 19. Clinical examination findings suggestive of TB include poor weight gain, severe acute malnutrition, pneumonia not responding to antibiotics, persistent wheeze, and specific physical signs such as enlarged lymph nodes, spinal kyphosis, or pleural effusion. 20. Weight loss or failure to thrive in children should prompt evaluation for TB. Growth faltering, static weight, or weight loss over time are key indicators. 21. Other causes of chronic lung disease, such as HIV infection, lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis, bronchiectasis, or asthma, should be considered and differentiated from TB. 22. A decision to start TB treatment based on clinical parameters should not be delayed if necessary investigations are unavailable, particularly for children at higher risk of severe disease, such as those under two years of age, living with HIV, or hospitalized with pneumonia unresponsive to first-line treatment. 23. A trial of TB treatment with anti-TB medications is not recommended as a diagnostic method in children.
